abstract: ABSTRACT Bottlenose dolphins produce several types of whistle contours, including signature whistles, shared whistles, copies of conspecifics' signature whistles, and variant whistles. While signature whistles as individual identifiers are well studied, less has been demonstrated for identifying dolphins from non‐signature whistle types. Shared whistles, which are produced by multiple dolphins, and signature whistle copies are particularly difficult to classify. Variant whistles remain largely unexplored for individual identification. This study evaluated the use of a convolutional neural network operating on raw amplitude vectors to classify which dolphin produced the whistle (20 different dolphins), regardless of the contour type, from the raw time‐series of whistle recordings. When trained on all whistle types, the model achieved strong performance in classifying whistle producers (85.20%), with the highest accuracies for signature (96.10%) and shared whistles (92.50%), moderate accuracy for variant whistles (72.10%), and lowest accuracy for signature whistle copies (17.20%). To evaluate the trade‐off between classification accuracy and ecological relevance, a model run solely on signature whistles achieved 93.70% accuracy. This study represents a first step toward caller identification across whistle types for well‐studied populations, rather than solely relying on individually unique signature whistles alone. These results also demonstrate the potential for deep learning (DL) and raw audio time series to support future advances in passive acoustic monitoring of odontocetes.
title: Identifying Dolphin Whistle Producers With Deep Learning: Moving Beyond Signature Whistles

abstract: ABSTRACT Animal rhythms are gaining increasing attention in the studies of behavior and musicology. Recently, it has been shown that rhythm itself can be used as an information coding channel. Now we ask: Does this hold true for arrhythmic sequences? To answer that, we analyzed songs of the tawny pipit ( Anthus campestris ), a migratory songbird known for its simple, arrhythmic songs. From focal recordings of 341 males across 6 European populations, we extracted an extensive set of rhythmic and temporal indices. We show that despite their apparent randomness, tawny pipit songs carry individual signatures—modern rhythmic indices such as beat precision and integer ratios proved among the most individually distinct parameters. Strikingly, we also uncover population‐specific temporal patterns across the species' European range that have not been revealed by conventional spectral analyses. This study is the first to demonstrate geographic scale differences in birdsong rhythm, and to show that rhythmic analysis can provide useful descriptions of arrhythmic sequences.
journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
title: Unique Rhythmic Signatures in Arrhythmic Birdsong

abstract: Blue whales produce stereotyped songs that are declining in fundamental frequency worldwide. We examine inter- and intra-annual frequency variation in the New Zealand population, which can be monitored year-round in the South Taranaki Bight. We document a decline of 0.13 Hz/yr between 1964 and 2025, and 0.08 Hz/yr between 2016 and 2025. Furthermore, we demonstrate higher fundamental frequencies from February to June, and a significant positive relationship between fundamental frequency and the song intensity index. These results indicate that blue whales sing at higher fundamental frequencies during the putative breeding season. Future work should aim to resolve relationships between song and morphological, demographic, behavioral, and cultural factors.
title: Inter- and intra-annual variation in the frequency of blue whale songs in Aotearoa New Zealand

abstract: A Rényi spectral entropy is introduced for environment-adaptive detection of underwater acoustic signals in low signal-to-noise conditions. The Rényi order α is a control parameter; varying α enhances contrast between signals and background noise and improves detectability. The entropy variance as a function of α exhibits four regimes separated by crossover points, from which an optimal interval for signal selection is identified. This establishes α as a single tunable parameter to optimize detection performance. The approach is validated on passive recordings of North Atlantic right whale gunshots and outperforms a detector based on the Shannon spectral entropy.
title: Rényi entropy-based detection of North Atlantic right whale gunshot vocalizations

abstract: North Atlantic minke whales (Balaenoptera acutorostrata acutorostrata) were acoustically detected and localized in real-time for 3.5 h off Jacksonville, Florida. During 1 h of this encounter, an individual was visually and acoustically tracked. Manual review of the recordings identified continuous low-frequency pulse trains (40-674 Hz). Not all pulse trains observed have been documented previously in the North Atlantic. Variation in frequency, duration, and the combination of known pulse trains were documented. The tracked whale also altered its calling behavior while the research vessel was present. These data provide insight into the acoustic behavior of minke whales in their winter habitat.
title: Vocalizations of North Atlantic minke whales ( Balaenoptera acutorostrata acutorostrata ) with direct visual observation off Florida

abstract: Bioacoustic data from passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) generates large datasets where obtaining detailed auditing and labelling is often impractical, resulting in weak annotations (e.g., presence/absence of species over several minutes of recording). In order to effectively capture the complex temporal patterns and key features of long audio segments, we propose a framework comprising dataset standardisation, feature extraction, and classification via temporal convolutional networks (TCN). This approach eliminates the necessity for setting heuristic decision rules or creating time-consuming strong labels. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we use sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) click trains in 4-min recordings as a case study, from a dataset comprising diverse sources and deployment conditions to maximise generalisability. Our TCN classifiers achieve recall rates exceeding 0.83 at a 0.13 false positive rate, comparable to agreement rates between expert annotators. We compare two methods of feature extraction, variational autoencoders (VAEs) and traditional handpicking of features, and found them to yield similar performance results, with the VAE-based classifiers seeing a more stable performance across datasets and recording conditions. These results offer a way forward in leveraging numerous existing annotated bioacoustic datasets to train automatic classification models, effectively overcoming previous limitations associated with weak labels.
journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
title: Classifying bioacoustic data without individual call annotations using temporal convolutional networks and feature extractors

abstract: Mitochondria are highly dynamic signaling organelles that engage in continuous bidirectional communication with the cytoplasm and participate in biological processes such as cell death, inflammation, and epigenetic modification. Mitochondria receive, process and export various types of signals, ranging from metabolites to non-coding RNAs. Despite their central importance, progress in understanding mitochondrial signaling has been hampered by the fragmented characterization of their communication networks. In this study, we present MitoCommun, a manually curated database comprising 580 mitochondria-derived signaling events from five model species: Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and Caenorhabditis elegans. Specifically, MitoCommun features 233 well-annotated mitochondrial signaling molecules, defined by either mitochondrial origin or specific organelle localization. These molecular entities have been systematically paired with their receptors and functionally mapped into explicit pathways and interaction networks. Furthermore, we have reconstructed signaling networks across phylogenetically divergent species, functionally distinct biological processes, and inter-organelle communication systems, yielding comprehensive topological maps of mitochondrial signaling cascades. By integrating these resources, MitoCommun establishes a foundational framework for decoding mitochondrial communication and serves as a versatile, user-friendly platform for exploring organelle signaling networks, which is freely accessible at http://mitocommun.qscn.online/ .
title: MitoCommun: a database for decoding mitochondrial communication networks

abstract: If you're a fan of comparative physiology, clicking on a new issue of Journal of Experimental Biology can feel like being let loose in an opulent store of treats. From stories about surfing zooplankton and caterpillar sound effects to the map sense of turtles and the impact of climate change, you can never be sure what you'll get, but it will be extraordinary. ‘JEB's strength lies in embracing diversity, from the animals studied, questions asked and approaches taken’, says Craig Franklin, JEB Editor-in-Chief. Behind each remarkable piece of research lie the personal stories of the early-career scientists that nurtured animals and painstakingly recorded their behaviour and physiology. ‘Supporting early-career researchers is fundamental to JEB's identity and our investment in the future of comparative physiology and biomechanics’, says Franklin. Each year, JEB recognises the achievements of the journal's early-career researchers, who make immense contributions to the research published in the journal, through the JEB Outstanding Paper Prize. Launched in 2005 in memory of former JEB Editor-in-Chief Robert (Bob) G. Boutilier, the shortlist provides a glimpse of the diverse topics covered by the journal, introducing the early-career researchers behind each remarkable discovery. The 2025 shortlist is a treat of scientific delight, revealing the creativity and ingenuity of the early-career researchers that brought each study to completion (Box 1). Box 1. Shortlisted articles for the 2025 JEB Outstanding Paper PrizeN. D. Antonson, S. Ogunbiyi, M. Champigneulle, T. J. Roberts, F. Goller and M. J. Fuxjager: Neuromuscular coordination of movement and breathing forges a hammer-like mechanism for woodpecker drilling.O. E. Demuth, J. R. Hutchinson, V. La Barbera, S. E. Warner and D. J. Field: Soft tissue constraints on joint mobility in the avian shoulder.D. Giacometti and G. J. Tattersall: Behavioural evidence of a humidistat: a temperature-compensating mechanism of hydroregulation in spotted salamanders.J. L. Huisken and S. M. Rehan: Transcriptomic correlates of nutritional manipulation in a facultatively social bee.K. Q. Karkosiak, R. Z. Schwartz, H. King and T. A. Blackledge: Spider egg sacs reveal how pockets of air can be used to conserve water.S. D. Lee, S. Wang, D. Kuang, E. K. Wang, J. K. Yim, N. H. Hunt, R. S. Fearing, H. S. Stuart and R. J. Full: Free-ranging squirrels perform stable, above-branch landings by balancing using leg force and nonprehensile foot torque.A. M. Martin, D. Cordero-De La Cruz and L. Swierk: High dissolved oxygen extends dive duration and suggests physical gill use in a vertebrate.T. Mulder, Y. Yang, E. Morley, T. E. Miller, D. Hending, G. K. Taylor and B. Mortimer: Constraints on percussive seismic signals in a noisy environment by European fiddler crabs, Afruca tangeri.A. B. Thies, M. Rangarajan-Paul, D. Wangpraseurt and M. Tresguerres: Co-option of immune and digestive cellular machinery to support photosymbiosis in amoebocytes of the upside-down jellyfish Cassiopea xamachana.In the first of the shortlisted papers (Antonson et al., 2025), Nicholas Antonson (Brown University, USA) and colleagues from Brown University and The University of Utah, USA, investigated how downy woodpeckers (Dryobates pubescens) coordinate and control their muscles and breathing while pecking wood. ‘This project was something that I had long wanted to do’, says PI Matthew Fuxjager, who worked with Antonson during his postdoctoral fellowship. ‘Nick's quantitative skills are very impressive’, says Fuxjager, recalling that Antonson figured out how to visualise and analyse the complex data to test their ideas about how woodpeckers use their muscles during their forceful impacts. ‘This paper stood out for me for a few reasons’, says nominating Editor Katie Gilmour, adding that the experiments performed by Antonson – recording muscle electrical activity and air-sac pressure while the birds were actively moving and drilling wood – were extremely challenging.Switching focus from a unique activity performed by a few bird species to an almost ubiquitous manoeuvre performed by most – wing flapping – Oliver Demuth and Daniel Field (University of Cambridge, UK) with John Hutchinson and colleagues from the Royal Veterinary College (RVC), UK, investigated the range of motion of the partridge shoulder joint (Demuth et al., 2025). ‘The impetus for the study is the perennial challenge of drawing robust conclusions about joint range of motion for extinct vertebrate animals’, says Field, explaining that simulations of the movements of fossil joints, including the soft tissues that have been lost, are essential to understand the evolution of modern birds. Describing how Demuth delicately manoeuvred the partridges’ shoulder joints in an X-ray machine to follow the full range of motion, Hutchinson recalls how Demuth then painstakingly analysed the joint's movements in 3D with support from Vittorio La Barbera and Sharon Warner (both at RVC). ‘This study offers major strides in revealing the essential roles played by the soft tissue in a single joint's mobility using a cutting-edge integration of computational modelling and sophisticated experimental measurements’, says nominating Editor Matt McHenry.In the next shortlisted article, nominated by Craig Franklin, Danilo Giacometti and Glenn Tattersall from Brock University, Canada, investigated the ability of amphibians to regulate hydration (Giacometti and Tattersall, 2025). ‘This study stands out for revealing an unexpected sensory mechanism in that salamanders appear to detect rates of evaporative water loss itself, not just ambient humidity’, says Franklin. Reflecting on Giacometti's role in the study, Tattersall says, ‘Danilo was the primary drive for the research, writing and design’, adding that he was impressed by Giacometti's ‘willingness to pursue difficult, cross-disciplinary questions requiring mastery of biophysical, physiological and behavioural concepts’. Having overseen peer review of the research, Franklin is excited by the study because it, ‘transforms our view of amphibian hydro-regulation from passive tolerance to active, informed behavioural regulation’.Moving from the realm of amphibians to the insect world, the next article shortlisted for the JEB Outstanding Paper Prize explores the mechanisms underlying the extraordinarily cooperative social structure of eastern small carpenter bees (Ceratina calcarata). In their study, Jesse Huisken and Sandra Rehan investigated whether diet underlies the role differences between dwarf eldest daughters, which are small and destined to serve their younger sisters, and regular sisters that have the potential to go on and found future colonies (Huisken and Rehan, 2025). However, when the duo investigated the differences in brain gene activation between the two castes, they realised that social experience and environment have more of an impact on the firstborn's destiny than diet or birth order. ‘This study stood out because it goes beyond simple correlative analysis to do an experimental manipulation and then track impact at the transcriptomic level to understand the mechanisms underlying the observed changes in social roles’, says nominating Editor Trish Schulte.From bee youngsters to spider eggs, nurturing the next generation is a key JEB theme. In their shortlisted paper, Katherine Karkosiak and Todd Blackledge (The University of Akron, USA) with Ravi Schwartz and Hunter King (Rutgers University – Camden, USA) investigated the permeability of spider egg sac silk, to determine how much protection the silk offers eggs from dehydration (Karkosiak et al., 2025). ‘We show that even though egg sacs look solid to our eyes, water vapour easily moves across them through tiny holes’, says Blackledge, which was a surprise. The team eventually realised that the egg sacs protect the eggs within by slowing the diffusion of water across the gap between the eggs and silk case and by shielding the eggs from moving air. ‘What makes this article exceptional is the authors’ systematic approach to answering a biological question’, says Franklin. And Blackledge, the PI on the study, was impressed by Karkosiak's resilience. ‘Kate showed immense scientific grit by transforming initial “failure” into a key insight for how water vapour moves across porous surfaces’, he says, adding that Schwartz's development of the physical model that explains how water diffuses through porous structures was a fantastic example of ‘integrated teamwork at its best!’.In a remarkable study investigating the landings of free-ranging fox squirrels on the University of California, Berkeley campus (USA), students Sebastian Lee, Stanley Wang and Duyi (Tina) Kuang – at Berkeley at the time – trained wild squirrels to jump into a rig that could measure the forces exerted as they touched down, to learn how squirrels, which land palm down on branches, avoid slipping off during botched landings (Lee et al., 2025). When the squirrels misjudged a short landing and overshot, they extended their rear legs, increasing their inertia to brake and prevent themselves from toppling forward. In contrast, the squirrels that undershot when trying to land a leap that was too far pulled themselves into a faster moving tight ball to swing themselves back up onto the branch. PI Robert Full says, ‘The students’ efforts paid off by discovering the secrets of dynamic balance, leading to the first legged robot that could land upright on a branch’. And nominating Editor Monica Daley says that she liked the paper because, ‘it involved challenging and creative experiments that required ingenuity and patience to collect data from wild animals using custom instrumentation’.An extraordinary investigation by graduate student Alexandra Martin and Lindsey Swierk (Binghamton University, USA) and then-undergraduate Diane Cordero-De La Cruz (University of California San Marcos, USA) reveals that water anoles (Anolis aquaticus) may be the first terrestrial vertebrate to breathe oxygen from water using a bubble as a physical gill to extract the gas from water (Martin et al., 2025). Filming the anoles submerged in normal, poorly oxygenated and super-oxygenated water as the reptiles rebreathed oxygen from an air bubble clinging to their foreheads, the researchers obtained several pieces of evidence suggesting that the bubble could be absorbing oxygen from the surrounding water to supplement the anoles’ oxygen supply. ‘Allie led this work as part of her doctoral dissertation’, says Swierk, adding that Martin invested a great deal of persistence and creativity, while Cordero-De La Cruz showed exceptional promise as an undergraduate researcher. JEB Editor Almut Kelber, who oversaw peer review of the research, said, ‘I like their simple but convincing and well-controlled experiment, their tests in more realistic environments with fast or gently flowing water and their caution pointing out that more data may have to be collected’.Editor Sheila Patek's nomination for the 2025 JEB Outstanding Paper Prize shortlist investigated the messages communicated by male European fiddler crabs when they beat the sand with their claws and drop their bodies to pound the sand (Mulder et al., 2025). Tom Mulder, Ellen Morley and Thomas Miller (University of Oxford, UK) recorded over 8000 percussive crab serenades with geophones embedded in a Portuguese beach over 2 months, revealing that the crabs with the largest claws stood out from the crowd by producing the loudest thuds. In addition, the percussive beats were not tuned to a particular tone, which could be an advantage in the noisy environment of the seashore, where wind and waves could drown out certain tones. ‘Tom led most aspects of this paper from inception to write up. This was particularly impressive given this was his first piece of academic fieldwork’, says PI Beth Mortimer (University of Oxford). And Patek pays tribute to the work saying, ‘This type of acoustic signalling in a noisy environment is very challenging to study, especially to disentangle individual effects and the interaction between the sound-producing mechanism and the changing environmental conditions’.In the final shortlisted paper of 2025, Angus Thies, Maitri Rangarajan-Paul, Daniel Wangpraseurt and Martin Tresguerres report how the cells that house symbiotic algae in the bodies of upside-down jelly fish have independently evolved the same mechanism as corals, anemones and giant clams to enhance algal production of sugars and oxygen, which are provided to the jellyfish (Thies et al., 2025). ‘There are so many cool things about this study’, says nominating Editor Pat Wright, who oversaw peer review of the article, recalling that the team used a variety of experimental approaches to unpick details about the ion transport mechanisms that permit the jellyfish to use algae kidnapped from their diet to directly fuel their tissues. PI Tresguerres is particularly proud of graduate student Thies, who also mentored Rangarajan-Paul during the research. ‘Angus did an amazing job, including contributing to the original idea and leading all of the experiments’, says Tresguerres.After reviewing the nine nominated research articles, the Editors are delighted to announce that Nicholas Antonson, Brown University, USA, has been awarded the 2026 JEB Outstanding Paper Prize for his paper, ‘Neuromuscular coordination of movement and breathing forges a hammer-like mechanism for woodpecker drilling’ (Antonson et al., 2025). ‘The story is both compelling and novel, an impressive winner of the JEB Outstanding Paper Prize’, says Gilmour, who nominated the paper for the award. Reacting to the news, Antonson exclaimed, ‘I was elated!’, adding that the award was completely unexpected.‘The project was something Franz Goller and I cooked up several years ago’, says Fuxjager. ‘We had been having conversations about motor coordination of drilling and drumming, debating how complex the mechanisms likely were’, he adds, explaining that they were curious to know whether drilling was a whole-body affair and whether breathing was involved at all. Joining Fuxjager's lab in 2023 as a National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellow, Antonson set about collecting eight of the tiny woodpeckers for a 3-day stay in the lab. Then he filmed their manoeuvres and recorded their muscle activity as they pecked and drilled a piece of hardwood. ‘The most challenging aspect of this research was getting all the different types of data – electromyography, respiratory pressure and high-speed video – to line up correctly so we could reconstruct a complete picture of how the woodpeckers coordinate movement with breathing during pecking’, says Antonson. And Fuxjager recalls that Antonson's ability to simultaneously handle and visualise the complex datasets to unpick the fine detail was impressive. ‘I think the most exciting moment was when we noticed that the woodpeckers were exhaling through each strike they were producing’, says Antonson. Effectively, the birds were grunting – like tennis stars each time they strike a ball – which likely helps to boost the power of each blow. Even more impressively, the woodpeckers were able to grunt up to 13 times per second when drumming on wood to assert territory or attract a mate: ‘It's kind of like a musician keeping a crazy-fast beat: if you can do it perfectly, people notice. Woodpeckers do the same thing and the best drummers stand out amongst their rivals’, Antonson explains.‘It's really rewarding to see a project that has been stewing for a very long time get honoured as a significant contribution’, says Fuxjager, and Antonson has been excited by the wider reaction to the paper. ‘I even had to act out what the rapid “grunting” sounded like during an interview on [US National Public Radio's] Science Friday, which gave my friends and family a good chuckle’, he smiles. Looking to the future, Antonson is excited by the prospect of setting up his own lab and Fuxjager is optimistic for his success; ‘Nick is a very creative scientist who is full of new ideas’, he says.Reflecting on the full Outstanding Paper Prize shortlist, Franklin is excited by the biological diversity that it represents, showcasing groundbreaking research in vertebrates and invertebrates with implications for palaeontology, biomechanics, physiology and neuroethology. ‘This shortlist captures everything I love about JEB’, Franklin says with a smile. And he is impressed by the determination and commitment of all of the early-career researchers whose work has been highlighted. ‘With scientists of this calibre coming through, the future of comparative physiology and biomechanics is in extraordinarily capable hands’, says Franklin, looking toward another exciting year of inspiration and discovery with Journal of Experimental Biology.
title: Announcing the 2025 Journal of Experimental Biology Outstanding Paper Prize shortlist and winner
why: species only in the abstract, title not about communication

abstract: Male mosquitoes locate females through strong and innate attraction to female flight sounds, the basis of mating in the world’s deadliest animal. In contrast, females do not show any sound attraction behaviors. Despite being documented for almost a century, the molecular underpinnings of these behavioral dimorphisms remain unknown. Here, we found that by disrupting the male-specific isoform of fruitless (referred to as fruM ) in Aedes aegypti , fruM mutant males show complete abolition of sound attraction behaviors, resulting in failure of mutant males to locate females for mating. We identified strong fruitless expression in control male ears, with the loss of FruM severely disrupting mutant male ability to amplify female flight sounds. fruM mutant male ears also propagate frequency-specific, sound-evoked electrical signals at about one-sixth the magnitude of control males, significantly reducing the amount of auditory information relayed to the brain. fruitless thus plays a significant role in determining proper male peripheral hearing function underlying mating. Transcriptomic analyses of mosquito ears identified essential hearing genes under the transcriptional influence of FruM via direct or indirect actions, thus shaping male-specific hearing cellular machineries that support male attraction to female flight sounds. Our work demonstrates that FruM commands male-specific hearing behaviors involved in mating by directly controlling the earliest stages of auditory organ performance, sound amplification and acoustic signal detection. Our findings show that FruM is essential for male-specific reproductive behaviors in mosquitoes.
title: fruitless is essential for male Aedes aegypti mosquito attraction to female flight sounds

abstract: Vocalizations provide an informative means of assessing the emotional states of animals, yet male vocal behaviour in domestic sheep remains unexplored. The study aimed to investigate whether rams' bleats vary across five distinct contexts associated with morning and night isolation, exposure to familiar ewe-bell sounds, feed anticipation, and feed denial. A total of 428 high-quality bleats were used to extract 20 acoustic parameters, which were then analyzed using a multivariate acoustic approach. Principal Component Analysis identified five independent acoustic components reflecting source-parameters, spectral energy, formant frequencies, voice stability, and temporal characteristics. Context significantly influenced the acoustic structure of bleats, with spectral, formant, vocal stability, and temporal characteristics showing context-dependent variation, whereas fundamental frequency-related parameters remained unaffected. Feed anticipation elicited higher formant-related scores; feed denial produced reduced spectral energy, and social isolation contexts were characterized by increased vocal instability. Discriminant analyses revealed moderate classification accuracy, indicating overlapping acoustic patterns and supporting graded rather than discrete vocal signals. Morphometric effects were minimal, with wither height affecting formant structure. The findings provide the first detailed evidence that rams modulate multiple acoustic features across contexts, demonstrating that male sheep encode emotional states through shifts in vocal parameter variation.
title: Investigating context-specific acoustic variation in the bleats of male domestic sheep

abstract: Understanding how primate frontal circuits encode socially informative vocalizations is central to elucidating the neural basis of communication. In common marmosets, functional MRI has identified robust selectivity for conspecific vocalizations in the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC; area 32), but the underlying neural dynamics driving this response remain unknown. Here, we investigated this by recording single-neuron activity in area 32 of five awake marmosets (three female and two male) using acute and chronic Neuropixels probes and Utah microelectrode arrays during presentation of a standardized cross-species auditory stimulus set comprising marmoset, macaque, and human vocalizations as well as a suite of nonvocal sounds. Of 1,713 neurons recorded across 17 sessions, 945 (55%) showed significant auditory responsiveness, and 362 (21%) were categorically selective. Selective neurons exhibited their strongest responses to marmoset calls, and population preference indices revealed a robust bias toward conspecific vocalizations. Temporal population analyses showed rapid encoding: decoding accuracy for detection of marmoset calls exceeded chance within ∼50-100 ms, and representational similarity analysis demonstrated that marmoset calls formed a distinct cluster separate from macaque, human, and nonvocal stimuli. These results provide the first direct evidence that ACC area 32 contains a specialized neural representation for conspecific vocal signals. By linking fMRI-defined selectivity to single-neuron population dynamics, our findings identify area 32 as a key node in primate vocal communication networks and illuminate how frontal circuits transform auditory input into socially meaningful categorical information.
title: Selective Neural Responses to Conspecific Vocalizations in Marmoset Area 32

abstract: Complex, learned motor behaviors involve the coordination of large-scale neural activity across multiple brain regions, but our understanding of population-level neural dynamics within different regions tied to the same behavior remains limited. Here, we investigate the neural population dynamics underlying learned vocal production in awake, singing songbirds. Using Neuropixels probes, we record simultaneous extracellular activity from populations of neurons in two regions of the vocal-motor pathway in adult male zebra finches. In line with observations made in non-human primates during limb-based motor tasks, we show that the population-level activity in both the premotor nucleus HVC and the motor nucleus RA is organized onto low-dimensional neural manifolds upon which coordinated neural activity is captured by temporally structured trajectories during singing behavior. Both HVC and RA latent trajectories carry relevant information to predict vocal sequence transitions between song syllables. However, the dynamics of these latent trajectories differ between regions. Our state-space models suggest a unique and continuous-over-time correspondence between the latent space of RA and vocal output, whereas the corresponding relationship for HVC exhibits a higher degree of neural variability. We demonstrate that high-fidelity reconstruction of continuous vocal outputs can be achieved from both spiking activity and neural latents. However, in contrast to models relying on spiking activity, decoding models leveraging latent dynamics generalize to novel subpopulations in each region, supporting the existence of preserved manifolds that confine vocal-motor activity in HVC and RA.
title: Population Dynamics in Songbird RA and HVC During Learned Motor-Vocal Behavior

abstract: Human-elephant conflict at forest boundaries has intensified significantly due to increased elephant herd intrusions into agricultural lands, resulting in substantial crop damage and adverse economic impacts on farming communities. This paper presents a comprehensive multi-modal approach combining Video Object Detection and Audio Action Classification (VODAAC) with a novel customized ResNetC4S2 (Resnet50 with CNN4 Skip2) architecture to address this critical challenge. Our system enables precise detection of individual elephants within herds, including occluded subjects, while simultaneously classifying their behavioural states (aggressive or calm) through audio analysis. The proposed ResNetC4S2 model incorporates optimized skip connections and residual blocks to overcome vanishing gradient problems while maintaining computational efficiency. For audio classification, extract mel spectrogram features that capture the distinctive acoustic signatures of elephant vocalizations, ranging from low-frequency rumbles (10-173 Hz) to high-frequency trumpets (4055879 Hz). Extensive evaluation using real-time datasets collected from Tirupattur forests demonstrates superior performance, achieving 85% mean Average Precision (mAP) in object detection and 97.1% accuracy in behavioural classification. Additionally, speed detection included for predictive analysis of potential intrusion trajectories. This integrated approach provides early warning capabilities with reduced false positive rates, facilitating timely interventions to mitigate human-elephant conflicts while ensuring the safety of both rural communities and wildlife.
title: ENHANCED DEEP RESIDUAL NETWORK ARCHITECTURE FOR REAL-TIME ELEPHANT (ELEPHAS MAXIMUS) INTRUSION DETECTION AND BEHAVIOURAL CLASSIFICATION USING MULTI-MODAL ANALYSIS
Last Calls of an Out-of-Habitat Killer Whale (Orcinus orca) in the Seine River

abstract: The chip call of the Eastern Wood-Pewee (Contopus virens) is a frequently cited feature of that species’ vocal repertoire, but similar calls of the Western Wood-Pewee (C. sordidulus) are usually overlooked. Differences in this call between the two species would aid in field identification of migrants, which rarely sing their diagnostic songs. Cross-correlations of audiospectrograms, comparisons of three audiospectrographic measures, and qualitative analysis of spectrograms show that most chip calls of the Eastern Wood-Pewee are not distinguishable from those of the Western Wood-Pewee, and Eastern chip calls are generally more variable than those of the Western. These analyses also show that the two wood-pewees are more similar to each other than they are to their respective sister taxa. This similarity raises questions about the role of chip calls in the behavior of Contopus species, especially as it relates to potentially shared functions and sources of selection in their nonbreeding ranges.
title: CHIP CALLS IN THE WESTERN AND EASTERN WOOD-PEWEES

abstract: Brood parasitism by the common cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) of its avian hosts is a classic model of coevolution. A previously published study proposed and provided experimental evidence supporting hypotheses about the function of the female common cuckoo's distinctive ‘bubbling’ call during parasitism. While acknowledging their methodological rigour and results, we highlight key evidence that challenges their conclusions about the role of the cuckoo’s vocalisation as a counter-defence strategy. In our study, we analysed 11 years of video surveillance data, combining 284 recordings of parasitism events from China and the Czech Republic at the nests of two major host species. Notably, female cuckoo vocalisation during parasitism was nearly absent (282 out of 284 cases). These data provide compelling evidence against the hypothesis that the bubbling call serves as a counter-defence strategy to deceive hosts. Moreover, two female cuckoos that vocalised at host nests were mobbed, further suggesting that the bubbling call does not misdirect host defences. Finally, we provide new insights into the proximate and ultimate factors that likely prevent female cuckoos from vocalising during parasitism, contextualised within recent research on brood parasitism.
title: Common cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) bubbling call does not serve as a counter-defence strategy in two warbler hosts in Europe and Asia

abstract: The endangered North Atlantic right whale (NARW) faces threats from lethal and sublethal stressors. Prey limitation has been linked to reduced growth and fecundity, while anthropogenic noise has been associated with acoustic behavior changes and increased physiological stress. We combined disparate data sets collected in Cape Cod Bay, Massachusetts, USA, across multiple years, quantifying links between prey, calling behavior, noise, and foraging behavior to answer 3 questions: (1) What are the characteristics of noise and prey density in the patches where NARW forage? Are prey density, call rate, and noise related to (2) the probability of being in a foraging state and (3) the size of the foraging group? We found links between predicted prey density and 2 measures of NARW foraging: probability of being in a foraging state and foraging group size. There were also significant non-linear relationships between lagged calling behavior and these same measures. For group size, an interaction term between calling behavior and prey density suggested a complex interrelationship between these variables. When more ambient noise was measured near a patch in the 4 h prior to a sighting of foraging whales, whales foraged in lower-quality zooplankton patches. Elevated noise ahead of aggregated sightings was also associated with a smaller group size. This is consistent with the hypothesis that increased ambient noise disturbs foraging and/or reduces communication space, limiting the ability of NARWs to fully exploit their environment. Our findings suggest pathways for future experiments to explicitly test the mechanisms underpinning foraging processes in endangered NARW.
title: Foraging behavior of Critically Endangered North Atlantic right whales is associated with ambient noise, prey density, and the acoustic behavior of conspecifics

abstract: Purple Finch ( Haemorhous purpureus ) populations in eastern and western North America differ in morphological traits and genetic characteristics, yet their vocal divergence has not been quantified. We analyzed flight-call structure in Eastern and Western birds using measurements of frequency and call duration. Multivariate analyses revealed strong acoustic differentiation between subspecies, driven primarily by differences in maximum frequency, minimum frequency, and frequency span. Duration was not significantly different. Variation among subspecies in flight call characteristics was much greater than variation within individuals or within subspecies. Discriminant function analyses correctly identified calls in 93% of samples that were originally identified by the recordist or by assignment based on known geographic ranges. The five misclassified birds were all recorded in the West, had been assigned subspecies status based on range, were detected only outside the typical breeding season and were statistically Easterns. After re-assignment, the chance of misclassifying a bird to the incorrect subspecies was near zero. Only one bird in our sample, recorded in the putative zone of overlap in the Pacific Northwest, was marginally intermediate in its frequency characteristics. The reliable identification of flight calls is useful because Eastern and Western Purple Finches are highly distinctive genetically and may warrant full species status. In addition, the growing popularity of public archives for bird sound recordings increases the possibilities to track movements of infraspecifically diverse taxa like Purple Finches that are highly vocal but whose plumage variation is subtle. Finally, the existence of structurally divergent calls suggests the possibility of broader ecological and evolutionary differentiation.
title: Flight calls of Eastern and Western Purple Finches (Haemorhous purpureus) are diagnostically different

abstract: Grey wolves ( Canis lupus ) rely on olfaction to communicate and acquire information about their environment. Olfactory signals delivered via urine, faeces, and glandular secretions, serve critical functions in reproduction, social interactions, and territorial defence. We studied the role of olfactory signals in mediating inter-pack conflict, a leading cause of mortality in free-ranging wolves, by exposing zoo-housed wolves to the scent of an unfamiliar individual, mimicking an intruder. We predicted breeding adults to exhibit higher investigatory and territorial behaviours, accompanied by an increased patrol effort in response to this simulated intruder than other individuals due to their dependence on territorial integrity and reproductive investment. Consistent with this prediction, breeders displayed significantly higher rates of investigatory, territorial and locomotor behaviours to conspecific than heterospecific urine than non-breeders. These findings highlight the specialised role that breeders play in wolf packs, particularly in relation to territorial defence, and demonstrate the deeply conserved patterns of territorial behaviours in wolves, even in populations that have been living under human care for a long time. Our findings have implications for theories of mammalian olfactory signalling and potential applications for conservation, including scent-based bio-fencing, to reduce human–wildlife conflicts.
title: Breeding status affects territorial behaviour to simulated intruders in captive wolves

abstract: Acoustic communication plays a fundamental role in coordinating social behaviors. From primates to elephants, social species use vocalizations to maintain contact, coordinate movement, and regulate social interactions. While the acoustic structure and contextual use of vocal signals have been widely studied, the temporal organization of vocal exchanges remains comparatively underexplored, despite increasing evidence that call timing carries meaningful social information and plays a central role in collective behavior. Here, we analyzed a dataset of semi-free African savanna elephants ( Loxodonta africana ) recorded in a standardized subgroup-separation context to elicit frequent contact rumbles. We applied three previously published methodological frameworks to the same dataset, each characterizing a different aspect of temporal coordination: quartile-based categories, bout criterion interval, and antiphonal probability analysis. We found that these statistical frameworks resulted in substantial variation in temporal boundaries and the classification of antiphonal signals, both within our dataset and relative to previous work. Quartile-based methods yielded shorter inter-call intervals, likely reflecting the high proportion of overlapping calls. Antiphonal probability analyses provided limited evidence for turn-taking across individuals. In contrast, bout criterion interval analysis revealed a comparatively longer temporal threshold, indicating that most vocalizations occurred within extended calling bouts. Overall, these findings demonstrate that methodological decisions strongly influence the identification and interpretation of temporal coordination, particularly antiphony, and can lead to differing conclusions about the presence and extent of coordinated vocal behavior. Consequently, given the limited number of existing studies on elephant vocal timing, early methodological choices may have a disproportionate impact on how temporal coordination is defined and detected, potentially shaping our understanding of coordinated vocal behavior in elephants.
title: Methodological frameworks influence the classification and interpretation of temporal coordination in African savanna elephant vocalizations

abstract: Introduction Bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops truncatus ) rely on whistle vocalisations for group cohesion and coordination. Although whistle characteristics are shaped by a wide range of factors, the combined effects of social structure, habitat characteristics and marine traffic remain poorly understood in the eastern Mediterranean. Methods This study investigated the acoustic ecology of bottlenose dolphins in the eastern Aegean Sea by integrating passive acoustic monitoring, photo-identification-based social network analysis, marine traffic ratio and environmental data collected between 2017 and 2025. A total of 986 whistles from 30 recordings were analysed. Results Individuals showed preferred associations, but modularity indicated that the nine detected clusters were not stronger than expected by chance, so clusters were considered tentative social units. Only the two largest clusters had enough independent recordings for acoustic comparison. When environmental variables were taken into account, whistle structure differed between the two clusters (PERMANOVA, R 2 = 0.29, p = 0.002). This result remained significant when accounting for group size and research vessel, and when excluding recordings shared by both clusters. Whistles of one cluster had more inflection points and a higher proportion of sinusoidal contours. Sea surface temperature was also associated with whistle structure, but this effect was not consistent across the robustness analyses and could not be fully separated from season. Marine traffic ratio, which was low throughout the study, showed no consistent effect on whistle structure, and depth had no effect. Social and environmental effects were only detected when considered together, suggesting that they may partly mask each other when examined separately. Discussion Whistle variation in bottlenose dolphins in the eastern Aegean Sea appears to be mainly related to social structure and, to a lesser extent, to environmental conditions, whereas no consistent effect of marine traffic was detected at the low traffic levels recorded. This study provides initial information on whistle variation in this population and its relationship with social and environmental factors, which can support future conservation and management strategies.
title: Relationships between social structure, environmental conditions and whistle characteristics in common bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) in the eastern Aegean Sea

abstract: Common bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops truncatus ) rely on whistles for group cohesion and coordination and on echolocation for prey detection and capture. In Texas bays, dolphins recurrently feed near shrimp trawlers and along seawalls, where they encounter different anthropogenic noises and prey availabilities. We used passive acoustic monitoring to compare whistles and click trains produced by dolphins foraging in these two human-modified habitats in the Texas Coastal Bend. Whistle sequences near trawlers exhibited greater contour diversity and complexity than those near seawalls, likely reflecting developmental and social influences within large mixed-age aggregations that included calves and young-of-year. Elevated group-level click and buzz activity near trawlers primarily reflected large group sizes rather than increased clicking by individuals, indicating collective echolocation effort. Higher proportions of buzz clicks and buzz-containing trains near trawlers indicate increased foraging effort and repeated prey-capture attempts when exploiting trawler-aggregated prey. Short, sparse, and more variable click trains near seawalls are consistent with exploratory echolocation in a less predictable foraging environment where the benefits of eavesdropping are reduced. The data show that social structure, prey resources, and habitat-specific noise shape communication and echolocation across the two foraging contexts.
title: Common bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) whistles and clicks across foraging contexts

abstract: Sperm whales ( Physeter macrocephalus ) produce powerful, broadband echolocation clicks that are used to detect and identify prey in deep ocean environments. Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) systems provide a non-invasive method to study the abundance of these animals, but face the challenge of false detections due to transient noise sources. In this paper, we propose a wavelet-based method to identify regions of interest (ROIs) containing sperm whale (SW) clicks by exploiting the impulsive characteristics of the clicks. A wavelet kernel is designed to match a Gabor function representing an SW click model. The signal reconstructed using this wavelet then produces high peaks primarily in ROIs containing SW clicks, while ambient noise and transient noise are suppressed. Compared with the commonly used Teager–Kaiser energy operator (TKEO) reference method and a reference wavelet-based SW click detection method, our work demonstrates a favorable trade-off between true and false detection rates for a large dataset of manually annotated SW clicks recorded near Dominica Island and the Bahamas.
title: A wavelet kernel design for the detection of sperm whale echolocation clicks

abstract: Nonhuman primates are essential model animals for understanding brain development and neurodevelopmental disorders. The common marmoset is becoming a key primate species due to its ease of handling and reproductive efficiency, along with increasing research resources, such as an MRI brain atlas of developing marmosets. The present study aims to further support the use of marmosets by providing a detailed description of the developmental trajectories of vocal behaviors with an automated system to detect and analyze vocalizations. We collected 64,736 vocalizations, classified them into 11 vocal types, and observed significant changes in their vocal behaviors from neonates to 12 weeks of age. Several call types, including Trill, Phee, and Cry, peaked around the sixth week before gradually declining. By contrast, calls such as immature Phee, and Twitter were most frequent at birth but decreased steadily, nearly disappearing by 6-8 weeks. In addition, we provide a platform for automatically detecting these vocalizations using artificial neural networks trained on a dataset applicable across various research contexts. Overall, this study not only describes the developmental trajectories of vocal behaviors in a fixed controlled context across developmental stages, but also serves as a reference framework for analyzing marmoset models of developmental disorders.
title: Developmental trajectories of vocal behaviors in common marmosets as a reference framework for neurobehavioral studies

abstract: Music is central to what makes us human. Yet, despite decades of research across cognitive science, archaeology, and evolutionary biology, there is no consensus on when human musicality first emerged. Musicality is the set of abilities required to perceive, produce, and appreciate music (Honing et al., 2015). Estimates for its emergence range drastically, depending on what one looks for: bone flutes appear in the archaeological record around 40 thousand years ago (kya; Conard et al., 2009). Meanwhile, theoretical models, e.g., of "musilanguage", a hypothesized ancestral communication system preceding language and music, suggest the roots of musical behavior date much further back (Brown, 2017, see also Mithen, 2006;Bannan, 2008;Fitch, 2010Fitch, , 2013)).While the exact moment musicality emerged remains elusive, recent genomic evidence allows us to establish a firm lower boundary: the latest point at which full-blown human musicality must have been present in our ancestral population, adapting the logic that Miyagawa et al. (2025) recently applied to language. Recent genetic and genomic studies of Homo sapiens lineages indicate that the first population divergence -marked today by the Khoisan lineages of Southern Africa -occurred around 135 kya (Lankheet et al., 2026;Ragsdale et al., 2023; see also the meta-analysis by Miyagawa et al., 2025). This provides a simple, but crucial heuristic. If full-fledged musicality had emerged only after this divergence, we would expect to find modern human populations that lack musicality, and/or whose musical systems lack fundamental structural elements.Yet no such population is known. Across regions and cultures, human music relies on shared perceptual and cognitive building blocks: using discrete pitch structures and scaled intervals grounded in tonal perception, alongside rhythmic entrainment and synchronized group dance grounded in metrical perception (Savage et al., 2015;Mehr, 2025). Cross-cultural comparative research suggests that while musical traditions vary, human listeners across disparate societies share core perceptual priors, such as biases toward simple integer-ratio rhythms and logarithmic pitch scales (Jacoby et al., 2019(Jacoby et al., , 2024)). The documented musical practices among Khoisan lineages, who are the deepest diverged branches in modern human genetics, similarly exhibit features depending on these foundational traits (Yende, 2024). Given the relative genetic isolation of this lineage, the vast presence of these traits indicates that the cognitive and physiological infrastructure required for musicality must have been operational prior to this ~135 kya split (though note that paleoanthropological findings point to potentially even around 300 kya; Hublin et al.,Having the biological infrastructure for musicality does not mean musical behavior appears automatically. Here, we distinguish between broad prerequisites (e.g., vocal motor control, auditory sequence processing) and full-fledged musicality; a composite trait comprising core cognitive systems for tonal and metrical perception (Honing et al., 2015;Mehr, 2025). While the underlying neurocognitive architecture must be music-ready, providing the raw biological capacity to acquire and process music (Seifert, 2018), musicality still depends on cultural environment and developmental exposure to unlock its full expression. So how far back do its building blocks extend? Genomic data establishes approximately 135 kya as a minimum date for modern Homo sapiens, but essential components of musicality and their biological prerequisites (e.g., vocal learning or cultural transmission) may have had distinct evolutionary histories, evolved gradually, and could predate our species altogether (e.g., Mithen, 2006;Clark & Henneberg, 2017;Podlipniak, 2025). The lineage split between Homo sapiens and Neanderthals occurred about 500 to 600 kya (Prüfer et al., 2014). Shared anatomical adaptations for vocal control and auditory processing (D'Anastasio, 2013;Martínez et al., 2004), alongside complex cultural transmission (Nielsen et al., 2020), indicate that hominins possessed key prerequisites for musicality prior to the >500 kya divergence.Whether these traits culminated in musical practice (e.g., Mithen, 2006;Podlipniak, 2025) or disputed artifacts like the Divje Babe bone item (Turk et al., 2018(Turk et al., , 2020;;contra: e.g., Diederich, 2015), remains unclear.Extending this phylogenetic perspective to our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos (genus Pan), reveals that several foundational components of musicalitysuch as rhythm production (Brooks et al., 2026;Hattori et al., 2026), timbre preferences (Kalan et al., 2019), potentially consonance preferences (Sugimoto et al., 2010), and joint acoustic coordination (Brooks et al., 2025) -are to some extent present in our primate kin.Alongside flexible gestural and vocal signaling (Liebal et al., 2004;Brooks et al., 2025), these shared traits reflect cognitive building blocks of human communication systems (Varella, 2023). The last common ancestor of hominines and Pan lived approximately 6-8 million years ago (mya; Coelho et al., 2026;Langergraber et al., 2012). Consequently, while full-blown musicality is found within our species, many of its key components likely rest on an ancient, shared heritage predating the Homo-Pan split.By combining genomic split-times with cross-cultural universals, we can reframe the timeline of human musicality. While ~ 135 kya represents the point by which musicality was present across our species, as we argue, its cognitive foundations are far older -a heritage that predates Homo sapiens itself.Allowing to date essential components of musicality offers fresh traction on longstanding evolutionary puzzles. For instance, a central debate in paleoanthropology concerns whether Neanderthals possessed speech (e.g., Boë et al., 2007vs. Lieberman, 2007). While vocal tract mechanics are often central to these disputes, musicality depends on a deeper suite of shared cognitive and physiological prerequisites (cf, Fitch et al., 2016): fine respiratory control, auditory sequence learning, precise sensorimotor integration, and social imitation. While our argument does not prove early hominins used acoustic communication systems, it suggests that their cognitive capacities -not just their physiology -would not have prevented them from doing so.More broadly, pushing the lower bound of human musicality back to at least ~ 135kya, and key components even further, offers two key theoretical advances to cognitive evolution. First, because music and language rely on similar foundational neurocognitive architecture (e.g., vocal motor control and auditory sequence processing; Asano et al., 2021Asano et al., , 2022;;Patel & Iversen, 2014;Rauschecker, 2014;Rauschecker & Scott, 2009;Zatorre et al., 2007), the genomic split around 135 kya holding for musicality corroborates the broader evolutionary premise for shared communicative capacities, and the proposed presence of linguistic capacity 135 kya (Miyagawa et al., 2025). Broadly, this timeline also intersects with linguistic estimates suggesting a Middle Stone Age origin for language (e.g., Perreault & Mathew, 2012). Second, musicality encompasses cognitive phenomena that language models fail to capture, such as discrete scaled pitch, octave equivalence, and rhythmic entrainment for group synchronization. Shifting the baseline for these traits from the 40 kya archaeological record to circa 135 kya provides evolutionary disciplines with a chronological anchor for modeling complex social-cognitive capacities. Material traces of prehistoric language are scarce, and archaeological evidence for abstract thought remains contested. However, because music is intrinsically bound to complex social cognition, emotional communication, and group synchronization, musicality as well as musical artifacts could act as a window into the ancestral mind.If we knew that full-blown music-readiness was locked in prior to early human population divergences, it would allow researchers across evolutionary psychology, linguistics, and anthropology to assume its underlying mechanisms were operational. We therefore suggest musicality as a foundational benchmark against which the emergence of other shared, high-level cognitive capacities, such as shared intentionality, narrative and poetic abilities, or cumulative cultural learning, can be modeled.Grounding the emergence of musicality in genomic divergence times provides a clear lower limit. While such genomic split times indicate a general baseline for specieswide cognitive infrastructure rather than a domain-specific genotype, pairing population genetics with cross-cultural universals situates human musicality to at least circa 135 kya, with building blocks likely extending past hominins to 6-8 mya.However, inferring ancestral biological capacity via present-day cross-cultural universality as a proxy for neurocognitive infrastructure requisitions caution. Beyond the genetic makeup discussed here, individual development may represent a critical interface between biology and culture (Laland et al., 2015) that may have shaped the evolution of human musicality (Patel, 2023;Savage et al., 2021). It also remains unclear how potential bio-cultural interactions during ontogeny integrate with other (co-)evolutionary factors, such as niche construction (van der Schyff & Schiavio, 2017) and inclusive inheritance.Empirically challenging this boundary offers an exciting pathway to resolve these ontogenetic uncertainties and advance our understanding of musicality. For instance, our proposed timeline would be challenged if cross-cultural research identifies a deeply diverged lineage that lacks and cannot acquire a core cognitive building block of musicality. Similarly, discovering lineage-specific divergences in developmental plasticity among modern children would indicate that the neurodevelopmental biases enabling modern musicality were not fully locked in prior to the ~ 135 kya split.Future research could further test and refine this benchmark, for instance, by also integrating paleoneurology (Asano, 2022), computational modeling (Haiduk & Popescu, 2026), paleogenomic dating of cognitive variants across hominin lineages (cf., Libedinsky et al., 2025;Zwir et al., 2022), and cross-cultural neuroimaging to clarify how musicality evolved alongside language and social cognition.Looking ahead, we suggest that musicality offers a crucial, empirical baseline for reconstructing the evolution of human mind and communication.
title: Musical capacity was present in Homo sapiens 135 thousand years ago: genomic lower bounds and the emergence of human musicality

abstract: Anthropogenic noise from Australia’s expanding Blue Economy, including shipping, fishing, and offshore renewable energy development, may impact pinnipeds on land and at sea, as they rely heavily on sound for communication, environmental sensing, and predator avoidance. Effective noise management requires species-specific hearing data. We present the first aerial audiograms of two Long-nosed fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri) between 100 Hz and 20 kHz, following a conditioned-response paradigm. Hearing tests were conducted inside an anechoic chamber at Taronga Zoo, Sydney. Both seals showed peak sensitivity at 3.2 kHz, with thresholds of 7 and 12 dB re 20 µPa. The younger female exhibited greater high-frequency sensitivity, while overall audiogram shapes were comparable to those reported for other (Northern) fur seals. Audiograms were overlain with spectra of common terrestrial noises and detection ranges were discussed. This study provides essential baseline data for developing auditory weighting functions, assessing the potential impacts of noise, and informing environmental management of coastal and offshore developments.
title: Aerial Audiograms of Two Long-Nosed Fur Seals (Arctocephalus forsteri)

abstract: Urban parks derived from historical forest fragments represent important refugia for biodiversity in rapidly expanding cities. The wood cricket, Nemobius sylvestris, was surprisingly found in a park in the northern part of Bucharest, Romania, an area under exponential residential development. The species was confirmed by calling song analysis and molecularly confirmed through DNA-barcoding. The acoustic analysis revealed substantial geographic variation in the signals of N.sylvestris across its European range, with the Romanian population exhibiting the most distinctive acoustic characteristics. A median joining network was constructed using available COI sequences from public databases, showing moderate genetic variability within European samples. This flightless, woodland-specialist cricket is highly sensitive to habitat fragmentation and its persistence in this urban park demonstrates the conservation value of retaining semi-natural forest structure within city green spaces. Our findings highlight the importance of urban parks as biodiversity refugia, particularly for habitat specialists with limited dispersal abilities. This discovery underscores the need for the integrative conservation management of urban forest remnants, emphasizing the retention of natural structural elements such as leaf litter and heterogeneous canopy cover to support diverse invertebrate communities.
title: Conservation Significance of Forest Remnants for Urban Biodiversity: Parks as a Refuge for the Wood Cricket, Nemobius sylvestris (Insecta: Orthoptera: Trigonidiidae)

abstract: Dolphins are widely recognized as intelligent marine mammals with sophisticated communication and echolocation. Accurately classifying their whistles is essential for understanding their communication patterns and monitoring their population size, structure, and distribution. In this study, we assembled a large, high-quality dataset of Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops aduncus) whistle signals collected at the Chimelong Ocean Kingdom. The dataset included multiple whistle categories, including a whistle type that has not previously been available for research. We then applied convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for classifying whistle signals, using five CNN architectures to analyze the signals. Model performance was evaluated using mean average precision (mAP), and the best-performing model achieved 0.929 in mAP on the test set, demonstrating that CNN-based approaches can effectively distinguish among different whistle classes. To probe robustness, we also introduced noise at defined SNR levels to increase testing complexity and assess the stability of the classifier. BELLHOP acoustic propagation modeling was used to generate channel impulse responses. These simulated signals were combined with the original signal data to construct an augmented training set. The results indicate that this augmentation enhanced the robustness of the classification model. Differentiating the whistle types is crucial as whistle categories may reflect variation in communication structure, behavioral context, or group-level acoustic patterns. Therefore, the proposed approach can support large-scale bioacoustic analysis and provide useful information for future studies on dolphin communication, behavior, and conservation.
journal: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
title: Advancing Dolphin Acoustic Monitoring: A Comprehensive Whistle Classification Framework

abstract: High-resolution seismic surveys are a growing source of underwater noise, posing potential risks to marine animals. While impact assessments and noise reporting are mandatory, no established, open-access software currently exists to support these tasks. To address this gap, a transparent, reproducible workflow for underwater noise impact assessments is presented, and demonstrated for a custom Sercel Micro-GI airgun and harbour porpoises in the Baltic Sea. This assessment reveals that impact zones are confined to tens of metres, significantly smaller than those typically assumed in energy industry surveys. The unweighted zero-to-peak sound pressure level is the most restrictive metric, with safety distances of 15 m to avoid permanent hearing damage, 20 m for temporary impairment, and 30 m to prevent behavioural disturbance. The signal falls below the Effective Quiet threshold beyond 700 m and becomes inaudible at 1250 m, minimising risks of cumulative exposure and masking. Key factors influencing safety distances include source level, directivity, auditory weighting, and geometric spreading. Conservative assumptions ensure precautionary estimates. The workflow is implemented in an open-source Python package, enabling automated impact assessment and reporting to national noise registries. Crucially, the package is designed to be extensible, allowing integration of future regulatory updates and scientific advance.
title: Is it too loud? Approximations for underwater noise impact assessments and reporting for high-resolution seismic surveys

abstract: The 1997/98 International Whaling Commission Southern Ocean Whale and Ecosystem Research (IWC‐SOWER) cruise was the third in a series of cruises undertaken to evaluate scientific techniques for differentiating between ‘true’ blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) and pygmy blue whales (B. m. brevicauda). Data were collected from skin tissue samples, acoustic recordings and behavioural observations. The cruise was supported by two vessels, the Shonan Maru No. 1 (SM‐1) and Shonan Maru No. 2 (SM‐2), provided by the Government of Japan. The research was conducted from 12 December 1997 through 9 January 1998 in an area off the west coast of Chile bounded by 18–40°S and 70–77°W. All whales studied on this cruise were visually identified by observers as pygmy blue whales. Sound recordings were obtained during 13 occasions when the SM‐1 vessel approached pygmy blue whales to obtain biopsy samples and identify the sounds produced. On eight of these approaches, a total of 20 calls were recorded, and these are unlike any calls previously recorded from pygmy blue whales off Chile. Call durations were between 2 and 60 s, and all calls had a fundamental frequency around 11 Hz and contained 2–5 harmonics. These results suggest that pygmy blue whales might respond acoustically by producing distress or alarm calls when approached by vessels, a novel acoustic behaviour observed for a mysticete. This study underscores the need for further acoustic research to better understand this phenomenon beyond this blue whale population.
journal: The journal of cetacean research and management. Special issue
title: Unique calls of the pygmy blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus brevicauda) recorded off the coast of Chile during the SOWER 1997/98 programme

journal: Revista Ibero-Americana de Humanidades, Ciências e Educação
title: FAUNA SILVESTRE: PERSPECTIVAS DE CONSERVAÇÃO EM AMBIENTE INSTITUCIONAL

abstract: This study examines how the violin can evoke, imitate, and transform the sonic behaviour of mosquitoes through ecological listening, biomimicry, and detailed timbral analysis. Recordings of Aedes aegypti and Anopheles gambiae flight tones were analysed to identify their narrowband frequencies, oscillatory patterns, and behavioural qualities. Through the lens of Soundscape Ecology, these insect sounds are treated as meaningful components of a wider acoustic environment rather than incidental noise. Biomimicry Theory then provides a framework for understanding how composers translate ecological behaviours, such as hovering, swarming, and darting, into violin gestures and textures. Using Spectro‑morphology, the study compares the spectral brightness, instability, and energy flow of mosquito tones with selected passages from works by Crumb, Saariaho, and Sciarrino, revealing points of acoustic and gestural convergence. Semiotic interpretation further shows how mosquito‑like timbres function as iconic, indexical, and symbolic signs, carrying cultural associations of fragility, tension, and presence. The findings introduce the concept of ecological timbre, demonstrating that environmental sound can shape instrumental expression and expand the violin’s role within a broader sonic ecology. The study contributes new insights to ecomusicology, biomimetic creativity, and contemporary music analysis.
journal: African Journal of Environment and Natural Science Research
title: Mosquitoes and the Violin: Ecological and Biomimetic Timbres in Contemporary Music
